summary: Jesus feeds about five thousand men, besides women and children, with a boy’s five loaves and two fish, and twelve baskets of leftovers are gathered.
key_insight: Jesus told the disciples, “You give them something to eat,” and He meant it. The miracle passed through their hands: they found the loaves, seated the crowd, served the food and gathered what was left.
story: The Twelve came back from their mission and told Jesus all they had done and taught. {Mk} News had just come that Herod had beheaded John the Baptist. {Mt} So many people were coming and going that they did not even have time to eat, so Jesus said, “Come aside by yourselves to a deserted place and rest a while.” {Mk}

They crossed the Sea of Galilee by boat to a quiet place belonging to the town of Bethsaida. {Lk} But the crowds saw them leave and ran ahead on foot from all the towns. When Jesus came ashore and saw the great multitude, He was moved with compassion for them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd. {Mk} He welcomed them, spoke to them about the kingdom of God, and healed those who needed healing. {Lk} It was spring. The Passover was near, and there was much grass in the place. {Jn}

Jesus turned to Philip and asked, “Where shall we buy bread, that these may eat?” He said this to test him, for He already knew what He would do. {Jn} As the day wore on, the Twelve urged Him to send the crowd away to find food and lodging. {Lk} Jesus answered, “You give them something to eat.” Philip reckoned that two hundred denarii worth of bread would not give everyone even a little. {Jn}

Andrew, Simon Peter’s brother, found a boy with five barley loaves and two small fish, “but what are they among so many?” {Jn} Jesus said, “Bring them here to Me.” {Mt} Then He had the people sit down in groups on the green grass, in hundreds and in fifties. {Mk}

Jesus took the five loaves and the two fish, looked up to heaven, blessed and broke the loaves, and gave them to the disciples to set before the people. {Mk} Everyone ate as much as they wanted. {Jn} Those who ate were about five thousand men, besides women and children. {Mt}
When they were filled, Jesus said, “Gather up the fragments that remain, so that nothing is lost.” They filled twelve baskets with the pieces of the barley loaves that were left over. {Jn}

The people said, “This is truly the Prophet who is to come into the world.” But Jesus knew they were about to take Him by force to make Him king, so He sent the disciples away by boat and went up the mountain by Himself alone. {Jn}
differences: John alone names Philip and Andrew, mentions the boy and the barley loaves, and notes that Passover was near.
In Matthew, Mark and Luke, the disciples raise the problem of food; in John, Jesus raises it with Philip.
Matthew alone adds “besides women and children.” Mark alone mentions the green grass and the groups of hundreds and fifties; Luke says groups of fifty.
Only John records the crowd’s attempt to make Jesus king.

fit.question: Who first raised the problem of feeding the crowd: Jesus (John) or the disciples (Matthew, Mark and Luke)?

points.label: A conversation, not one sentence
points.text: John records Jesus testing Philip as the crowd was arriving (John 6:5). The other Gospels record the Twelve coming to Jesus later, “when the day was now far spent” (Mark 6:35). Both exchanges happened.

points.label: The same numbers
points.text: Philip’s “two hundred denarii” in John matches the disciples’ question in Mark 6:37. The accounts dovetail rather than collide.

fit.note: Different witnesses remember different parts of a long afternoon. Each part fits the others.
fit.short: Jesus tested Philip as the crowd arrived; later the Twelve urged Him to send them away. John records one exchange, the others another.

fit.question: Luke places the feeding near Bethsaida. But Mark says that afterward the disciples crossed “to the other side, to Bethsaida” (Mark 6:45). How can both be true?

points.label: Two towns named Bethsaida
points.text: McGarvey and others held that the feeding was near Bethsaida Julias on the northeast shore, while the boat headed for a second Bethsaida, a fishing village near Capernaum (John 12:21 calls it “Bethsaida of Galilee”). John says they were heading toward Capernaum (John 6:17).

points.label: A short first leg
points.text: Others think the disciples set out along the shore toward Bethsaida Julias to wait for Jesus before heading on to Capernaum, and the storm that night drove them off course (Mark 6:48, 53).

fit.note: The Gospels do not tell us which explanation is right, and either fits the details. This is the kind of detail invented stories rarely bother to get right.
fit.short: The feeding was near Bethsaida on the northeast shore. Either there were two towns named Bethsaida, or the boat’s course went toward it first.

scene.label: Barley loaves
scene.text: Barley was the cheaper grain, the bread of the poor. These were small, flat loaves, a boy’s lunch.

scene.label: Two hundred denarii
scene.text: A denarius was a day’s wage for a laborer (Matthew 20:2). Philip was talking about more than half a year’s pay, and he said even that would not be enough.

scene.label: Green grass at Passover
scene.text: Mark mentions green grass and John says Passover was near. The hills of Galilee are green only for a short time in spring, a small detail that fits the season.

scene.label: Sheep without a shepherd
scene.text: The phrase comes from Numbers 27:17 and Ezekiel 34, where God promised to shepherd His people Himself. Jesus feeds and teaches the flock their leaders had neglected.

scene.label: Bread in the wilderness
scene.text: Every Jew remembered God feeding Israel with manna in the wilderness (Exodus 16). The next day, Jesus will say, “I am the bread of life” (John 6:35).

witnesses.matthew: Places the feeding right after the death of John the Baptist, so Jesus withdraws in grief and still meets the crowd with compassion and healing. He alone counts the women and children, which makes the crowd far larger than five thousand.
witnesses.mark: Shows Jesus as the Shepherd: the crowd like sheep without a shepherd, the green grass, the people seated in ordered ranks like Israel’s camp in the wilderness. Later Mark notes that the disciples “had not understood about the loaves” (Mark 6:52).
witnesses.luke: Links the feeding to the apostles’ return and to Jesus’ teaching about the kingdom of God. Luke moves straight from the feeding to Peter’s confession (Luke 9:18–20), so the question “Who is this?” is answered right after the bread.
witnesses.john: Counts the feeding among his signs, sets it at Passover, and names Philip, Andrew and the boy. In John it opens the long teaching on the Bread of Life and shows that the crowd wanted bread and a king on their own terms.

seeing.reveals: Jesus is the Shepherd who sees the crowd with compassion and the Lord who provides bread in the wilderness: more than enough, with nothing wasted.
seeing.living: Jesus still says, “You give them something to eat,” to disciples who know they do not have enough. Bring Him what you have, however small and ordinary, and let Him bless it and pass it through your hands.
seeing.ponder: What “five loaves” are you holding back because they seem too small for the need in front of you?

preaching.big_idea: Little in Jesus’ hands becomes more than enough.
outline: An offering that seemed too small (8–9)
A provision with more than enough (10–13)
A response that missed the point (14–15)
preaching.watch_for: This is the only miracle before the resurrection told in all four Gospels. In John it opens a chapter that moves from bread for the body to Jesus as the Bread of Life (John 6:35).
